findings.claim: Basis for every reproduction below: a scratch copy of the frozen loop-2 export (equal to HEAD 607eea16); the shipped starter gives 0/26 and its result lines equal expected/starter-summary.txt; the critic wrote its own passing solution (26/26 under node --test with LAB_PROJECT, result lines equal expected/solved-summary.txt), and each variant is a minimal edit of it, evaluated by calling every rule function in tests/lab.mjs that the 26 tests assert on (the key variants were also rerun through node --test with LAB_PROJECT, with the same counts). Loop 2 changed the no-guard message of reviews-auth-forward to "a request with no token would reach the shop api without one: answer 401 before the call when authorization is missing". That consequence is false for the plain dict-literal shape: a dict literal that maps Authorization to the optional parameter, passed as the call's headers, with no guard. In httpx 0.28.1 a None header value raises TypeError ("Header value must be str or bytes, not <class 'NoneType'>") before any request is sent. Executed under FastAPI TestClient against a local stub api, a request without the header returned 500, and the stub api received no request. The message is true only for the conditional-headers shape, which sent the request with no Authorization header and returned 200. The loop-1 message described the dict-literal case accurately (send None as the header and end in a 500). The same false message is also shown for the positive-form guard (if authorization ... else raise 401), which does answer 401; that false fail is recorded under ops-sme-r1-01.
findings.recommendation: Word the message so that it is true for both shapes. For example: "a request with no token would end in a 500 or reach the shop api without one: answer 401 before the call when authorization is missing". Alternatively, choose the wording by whether the headers expression is conditional.

findings.claim: Basis for every reproduction below: a scratch copy of the frozen loop-2 export (equal to HEAD 607eea16); the shipped starter gives 0/26 and its result lines equal expected/starter-summary.txt; the critic wrote its own passing solution (26/26 under node --test with LAB_PROJECT, result lines equal expected/solved-summary.txt), and each variant is a minimal edit of it, evaluated by calling every rule function in tests/lab.mjs that the 26 tests assert on (the key variants were also rerun through node --test with LAB_PROJECT, with the same counts). ci-permissions returns leastAccess(top) as soon as a top-level permissions block exists (line 586), and it never looks at jobs.<job_id>.permissions. Each of these one-line additions passes 26/26: a top-level contents: read plus "permissions: write-all" on the build job, and the same top-level block plus a build-job block of contents: read and packages: write. GitHub documents that a permissions key inside a job gives every action and run command in that job the access it lists, so the job that holds the registry secrets runs with a write-scoped GITHUB_TOKEN. Yet test 8 ("a permissions block gives GITHUB_TOKEN least access") passes. Loop 2 added per-job checking only for the case with no top-level block (lines 587-596), so the two paths are now asymmetric. The same override also passed under the loop-1 grader, so this is not a regression. It is low because the learner must add a write grant on purpose, and the README never suggests one, but GitHub's own Docker Hub publish example puts a job-level permissions block with packages: write and other write scopes on its push job.

evidence.section: permissions: "You can use permissions either as a top-level key, to apply to all jobs in the workflow, or within specific jobs. When you add the permissions key within a specific job, all actions and run commands within that job that use the GITHUB_TOKEN gain the access rights you specify."
Publishing images to Docker Hub: example workflow job push_to_registry with job-level permissions packages: write, contents: read, attestations: write, id-token: write

findings.recommendation: When a top-level block exists, also run leastAccess on every job that has its own permissions block, and fail with the existing least-access message. Keep the current per-job path for workflows that have no top-level block.

findings.claim: Basis for every reproduction below: a scratch copy of the frozen loop-2 export (equal to HEAD 607eea16); the shipped starter gives 0/26 and its result lines equal expected/starter-summary.txt; the critic wrote its own passing solution (26/26 under node --test with LAB_PROJECT, result lines equal expected/solved-summary.txt), and each variant is a minimal edit of it, evaluated by calling every rule function in tests/lab.mjs that the 26 tests assert on (the key variants were also rerun through node --test with LAB_PROJECT, with the same counts). commands() (lines 508-511) splits a run script on newlines, so in a heredoc the printer and the line that expands the secret are judged apart. Repro: a new build-job step whose run block is cat <<EOF, then a line holding the job-env variable mapped from secrets.REGISTRY_PASSWORD, then EOF. It passes 26/26. Run under bash -e with that variable set, the step writes the secret value to stdout, which is the run log. A heredoc is a redirection, and the r1-07 acceptance lists the here-string form as the minimum ("at least"), which holds. This shape is the remaining unflagged printer form beside printenv, which was ruled non-binding. The same behaviour existed under the loop-1 grader. It is low because an unquoted heredoc that prints a secret is a deliberate shape, not a slip the starter invites.
findings.recommendation: Before splitting, fold each heredoc body (from a <<WORD or <<-WORD operator up to its terminator) into the command that opened it, and treat any secret-mapped variable in the body as fed to that command. Alternatively, accept this shape explicitly as non-binding in the reconciliation, as was done for printenv.

Basis for every reproduction below: a scratch copy of the frozen loop-2 export (equal to HEAD 607eea16); the shipped starter gives 0/26 and its result lines equal expected/starter-summary.txt; the critic wrote its own passing solution (26/26 under node --test with LAB_PROJECT, result lines equal expected/solved-summary.txt), and each variant is a minimal edit of it, evaluated by calling every rule function in tests/lab.mjs that the 26 tests assert on (the key variants were also rerun through node --test with LAB_PROJECT, with the same counts). Every case the acceptance names behaves. Must fail, and does: an unused lowercase local named timeout with no timeout on the call ("built but never used"); the same plus a plain number on the call (single-number message); an unused Timeout bound to another name; read=None; connect=None. Must pass, and does: a Timeout inline in the call; one bound to a module-level name and passed by that name; one bound to a local named timeout and passed by it; one given to the httpx.Client whose client.get makes the call (with-block); an async AsyncClient. One acceptance sentence still fails: "only a timeout keyword argument inside a call's argument list counts as passing a timeout, for the outgoing httpx call or the httpx client it uses". keywordArgs (lines 258-278) and line 286 count a timeout= keyword on any call except httpx.Timeout. Repro: a module-level httpx.Client built with the Timeout and never used, while the httpx.get call has no timeout, passes 26/26. The pass is wrong because the request runs on HTTPX defaults, not the explicit connect and read limits the test title promises. Residual severity: low. HTTPX's default timeout still bounds the call, so nothing hangs, and the slip needs a client the learner builds but never calls. Fix: count the keyword only on the call that outgoingCall identifies, or on a client whose name makes that call.

Basis for every reproduction below: a scratch copy of the frozen loop-2 export (equal to HEAD 607eea16); the shipped starter gives 0/26 and its result lines equal expected/starter-summary.txt; the critic wrote its own passing solution (26/26 under node --test with LAB_PROJECT, result lines equal expected/solved-summary.txt), and each variant is a minimal edit of it, evaluated by calling every rule function in tests/lab.mjs that the 26 tests assert on (the key variants were also rerun through node --test with LAB_PROJECT, with the same counts). All five must-fail variants fail. A guard body that prints, an HTTPException created without raise, and a guard returning a dict all get the missing-raise message (line 352). A removed guard with the headers made conditional on authorization, inline or through a name, fails (line 350). A forwarding dict built but not passed, with the call sending an empty dict, fails (line 343). The named must-pass forms pass: a dict literal in the call's headers, a name assigned the dict, a subscript-built dict, a lowercase key, a not-authorization guard with status_code=401, a status.HTTP_401_UNAUTHORIZED constant, and a required parameter with no guard. Two acceptance sentences still fail on runnable code. (1) "It passes a guard on missing authorization whose body raises HTTPException with 401 before the outgoing call": RAISE_401 (line 335) needs 401 or status_code= right after the opening parenthesis. raise HTTPException(detail=..., status_code=401) therefore fails with the false message "does not raise HTTPException with 401", although handlers() at line 364 already accepts any keyword order. The positive form, if authorization: build the headers, else: raise HTTPException 401, fails with "a request with no token would reach the shop api without one", because line 349 recognises only not-authorization or is-None guards. (2) "With the forwarded value reaching the call ... through the name assigned that dict ... and passed as headers": this fails when the URL is in a local variable, or when a base_url client makes the call, because outgoingCall (lines 311-322) then finds no call or the wrong one (details under ops-sme-010). Executed under FastAPI TestClient against a local stub api, every one of these shapes forwards the token and answers 401 without calling the api when the header is missing. All of them pass 26/26 under the loop-1 grader, so these are regressions introduced by loop 2. Residual severity: medium. The false messages give the learner no route to a fix.
